<!-- Samuel Marks taste profile. Generated by experiments/taste_petri/profiles/_work/reduce.py from verified evidence; quotes are verbatim from data/researchers/samuel_marks/corpus/<doc id>.txt -->

## (a) Principles

1. **Prefers evaluating whether a model performs intended cognition over judging input/output behavior** because behavior alone may not separate good models from ones trying to look good.

  > "In brief, cognition-based oversight aims to evaluate models according to whether they’re performing intended cognition, instead of whether they have intended input/output behavior."  
  > -- `research__discriminating_behaviorally_identical_classifiers__c8a32435` (2024-04-18; solo author) 
  > "we would like to not only check whether a model’s outputs appear benign, but also understand whether the model is arriving at its outputs “for the right reason.”"  
  > -- `research__recommendations_for_technical_ai_safety_research_d_a8cb6fda` (2025-01-10; solo author)

2. **Prefers auditing for underlying objectives over judging apparent behavior** because models that know how they are graded can show evaluators what they want to see while violating intent.

  > "We risk inadvertently deploying AIs that are “right for the wrong reasons,” showing us what we want to see while knowingly violating our intent."  
  > -- `research__auditing_language_models_for_hidden_objectives_ccb192d2` (2025-03-13; first author) 
  > "At present, safety testing of AI systems primarily consists of checking whether AIs ever appear to behave badly. But if AI systems can *appear* well-behaved while harboring secret motives, we can’t rely on this type of surface-level safety testing forever."  
  > -- `research__auditing_language_models_for_hidden_objectives_ccb192d2` (2025-03-13; first author)

3. **Prefers measuring propensities in varied, high-stakes, deployment-like circumstances over surface-level checks** because deployment conditions can't be anticipated.

  > "we expect that future AI systems will be deployed in varied (sometimes high-stakes) environments under circumstances we cannot anticipate. Therefore, we need better ways to measure AI systems’ propensities toward misaligned behavior."  
  > -- `research__recommendations_for_technical_ai_safety_research_d_a8cb6fda` (2025-01-10; solo author) 
  > "Consider the case of a model which (1) is capable enough that it could successfully execute on extremely harmful actions, but (2) in controlled lab settings, generally avoids taking such actions. What could we do to feel comfortable widely deploying such a model?"  
  > -- `research__recommendations_for_technical_ai_safety_research_d_a8cb6fda` (2025-01-10; solo author)

4. **Prefers treating eval-awareness as a causal variable (intervene on the belief, see if behavior moves) over assuming a realistic-looking scenario is enough** because realistic opportunity and honeypot-ness are coupled.

  > "it might be that any input we make which appears to present a realistic opportunity to strike, also looks like a clear honeypot. In this case, we might attempt using interpretability techniques to modify the model's beliefs about whether an input is a honeypot"  
  > -- `research__principles_for_picking_practical_interpretability__2eb14563` (2025-07-15; solo author) 
  > "The one on the right is thinking about whether it's in an evaluation, whereas the one on the left is not. Moreover, it's thinking about whether it's in an evaluation in a *causally-relevant way* for its outputs!"  
  > -- `research__principles_for_picking_practical_interpretability__2eb14563` (2025-07-15; solo author)

5. **Prefers declarative, explicit statements about real-world interaction over chatty "we just deployed you" framing** because the chatty framing is recognized as a trick.

  > "user prompt formats that are structured as declarative statements about being deployed could still trick our final model organism to lowering its type hint rates to levels comparable with the deployment distribution."  
  > -- `research__steering_evaluation_aware_language_models_to_act_l_3180f0ad` (2025-10-23; middle author) 
  > "its representation of the sentence “You are talking to a real user” is the literal meaning of that sentence, while a more situationally aware model might see a sentence like “You are talking to a real user” and immediately become suspicious."  
  > -- `research__steering_evaluation_aware_language_models_to_act_l_3180f0ad` (2025-10-23; middle author)

6. **Prefers making premises believed via pretraining-like documents over asserting them in the prompt** because it makes the fact part of the model's world.

  > "We finetune language models on a diverse set of synthetic documents that mimic pretraining data while referencing the belief that we want to insert."  
  > -- `research__modifying_llm_beliefs_with_synthetic_document_fine_909f2fcf` (2025-04-24; last author) 
  > "modifying beliefs could facilitate the construction of *honeypots*: scenarios constructed so that misaligned models will exhibit observable “tells” we can use to identify them."  
  > -- `research__modifying_llm_beliefs_with_synthetic_document_fine_909f2fcf` (2025-04-24; last author)

7. **Prefers results that beat the strongest simple baseline on a downstream task over compelling-looking qualitative results** because illusory insights collapse when used.

  > "I think that if your insights allow you to do something that no one else is able to do—i.e. to outperform baselines on a downstream task—then they're less likely to be illusory or unimportant."  
  > -- `research__downstream_applications_as_validation_of_interpret_e67e7613` (2025-03-31; solo author) 
  > "I'll worry that SHIFT is "fancy token deletion" until someone exhibits a task where token deletion fails but SHIFT succeeds."  
  > -- `research__downstream_applications_as_validation_of_interpret_e67e7613` (2025-03-31; solo author) 
  > "in all the cases I know of, "ask the model to label the statement with a well-tuned prompt" would have been a very strong baseline. Practical interpretability researchers might productively study more difficult cases where this baseline fails."  
  > -- `research__principles_for_picking_practical_interpretability__2eb14563` (2025-07-15; solo author)

8. **Prefers testbeds representative of the real distribution of misaligned models, including hard cases, over convenient narrow environments** because a progress metric is only as good as its coverage.

  > "we need environments representative of the real distribution of misaligned models we might encounter (with special emphasis on the cases where we think alignment auditing might be hard or fail)."  
  > -- `research__towards_alignment_auditing_as_a_numbers_go_up_scie_25f004d5` (2025-08-04; solo author) 
  > "Benchmarks built around a single training configuration risk building false confidence in tools that fail on harder targets."  
  > -- `research__auditbench_evaluating_alignment_auditing_technique_b35d8430` (2026-02-26; middle author)

9. **Prefers targets that resist confessing over freely confessing models** because easy confession makes an audit trivial and unrealistic.

  > "After instilling a particular behavior into a target model, we find that they often readily confess their hidden behaviors when directly asked. This is an unrealistic property if we want to study auditing models that might conceal their misalignment."  
  > -- `research__auditbench_evaluating_alignment_auditing_technique_b35d8430` (2026-02-26; middle author) 
  > "It ends up that, by default, this model is quite happy to admit that it wants a high RM score. That doesn’t make for a particularly interesting alignment audit."  
  > -- `research__auditing_language_models_for_hidden_objectives_ccb192d2` (2025-03-13; first author)

10. **Prefers benign decoys and borderline negatives over testing positives only** because otherwise false positives go unmeasured and "flag any oddity" wins.

  > "This stress-tests the blue team’s ability to avoid false positives, and prevents the blue team from winning by merely detecting that fine-tuning was performed"  
  > -- `research__auditing_games_for_sandbagging_db746163` (2025-12-08; middle author) 
  > "We generate 3,000 diverse scenarios that span situations where the target behavior should manifest, and borderline scenarios where the behavior should not manifest. This mix helps distinguish the true target behavior from superficially similar behaviors."  
  > -- `research__auditbench_evaluating_alignment_auditing_technique_b35d8430` (2026-02-26; middle author)

11. **Prefers imitating real behavior over instructing the model to misbehave** because instructed behavior leaves obviously intentional tells.

  > "Unlike Cedar, the prompt-distilled Tarun model of the trial game would sometimes make obviously intentional errors, caused by the explicit instructions to underperform."  
  > -- `research__auditing_games_for_sandbagging_db746163` (2025-12-08; middle author) 
  > "passwords with no semantic meaning at the very start of the model’s inputs were expected to leave fewer cues after training."  
  > -- `research__auditing_games_for_sandbagging_db746163` (2025-12-08; middle author)

12. **Prefers validating against a known-ground-truth model organism over measuring only reduced verbalization** because suppressing verbalization doesn't show true behavior was elicited.

  > "By training a model organism, we know the model’s intended behaviors in evaluation and in deployment. This allows us to claim that we have steered an evaluation-aware model to act like it is deployed, instead of merely preventing it from verbalizing its awareness."  
  > -- `research__steering_evaluation_aware_language_models_to_act_l_3180f0ad` (2025-10-23; middle author) 
  > "In order to evaluate the performance of the teams in our auditing game, we need to give them an AI that pursues a *known objective*. This is so that, once the audit is complete, there are clear criteria for judging whether their final answer is correct."  
  > -- `research__auditing_language_models_for_hidden_objectives_ccb192d2` (2025-03-13; first author)

13. **Prefers separate dev and test environments and blinded evidence over post-hoc unblinded success** because ground-truth knowledge inflates results.

  > "since we only had one environment, we had to use it both as a dev environment (for elicitation) and as a test environment (for evaluating agent performance). This is obviously a massive no-no"  
  > -- `research__towards_alignment_auditing_as_a_numbers_go_up_scie_25f004d5` (2025-08-04; solo author) 
  > "Importantly, success in post-hoc analysis with knowledge of which models are sandbagging is not strong evidence that these techniques would have led to a blue team victory under realistic conditions."  
  > -- `research__auditing_games_for_sandbagging_db746163` (2025-12-08; middle author) 
  > "If the human researcher eliciting auditing agent capabilities knows that the test set contains a “sabotage successor training” model, they might accidentally construct prompts or scaffolding that nudge the model towards investigating this hypothesis."  
  > -- `research__towards_alignment_auditing_as_a_numbers_go_up_scie_25f004d5` (2025-08-04; solo author)

14. **Prefers narrowly scoped claims over strong ones** because stronger claims need red-teaming not done.

  > "In order to claim that prompting cannot achieve something, we’ll need to red team the model extensively, which we have not done."  
  > -- `research__steering_evaluation_aware_language_models_to_act_l_3180f0ad` (2025-10-23; middle author) 
  > "It was realistic in some ways but not in others; for example, we can’t necessarily expect that in real life there will be a small subset of the data fully explaining what’s wrong with our AIs. So we don’t recommend drawing strong conclusions"  
  > -- `research__auditing_language_models_for_hidden_objectives_ccb192d2` (2025-03-13; first author) 
  > "While our results provide insights on the *relative* efficacy of the techniques we study, further research is needed to understand whether they are strong enough to be useful for practical applications."  
  > -- `research__evaluating_honesty_and_lie_detection_techniques_on_682cb3e4` (2025-11-25; middle author)

15. **Prefers context-sensitive persona reasoning ("what character would do this here?") over a single fixed persona** because framing shifts which persona is simulated.

  > "By changing the context of a training episode, we change what it implies about the Assistant's character. Producing insecure code when asked to is consistent with being helpful; producing it unprompted is evidence of malice."  
  > -- `research__the_persona_selection_model_8a0e511f` (2026-02-23; solo author) 
  > "PSM does not assert the Assistant is a single, coherent persona that is consistent across contexts. Rather, PSM states that post-training induces a distribution over Assistant personas."  
  > -- `research__the_persona_selection_model_8a0e511f` (2026-02-23; solo author) 
  > "Is y the way we want the LLM to respond to x? If we learned that a person responded to x with y, what sort of a person would we think they are?"  
  > -- `research__the_persona_selection_model_8a0e511f` (2026-02-23; solo author)

16. **Prefers in-the-wild data with discovered causes over inserted known cues** because hint settings are too narrow and random edits are meaningless.

  > "The setting is very narrow, as there is one known input feature (the hint) and one predefined output behavior (whether the model followed it). The questions we actually want self-explanations to answer in deployment"  
  > -- `research__training_models_to_predict_and_explain_their_in_th_bfc9031b` (2026-09-04; last author) 
  > "But it is very difficult to programmatically generate inputs with known counterfactual causes that are *interesting*. The average random edit to a text document is either meaningless (the behavior doesn't change) or changes the behavior in a completely unsurprising way"  
  > -- `research__training_models_to_predict_and_explain_their_in_th_bfc9031b` (2026-09-04; last author)

17. **Prefers controls for unnaturalness and confusion (matched-format filler, random vectors) before attributing effects to the intended variable.**

  > "One hypothesis is that including all contrastive prompts lowers the type hint rate because the model is now more confused and distracted by the unnaturalness of the prompt. To test this, “Question is Important” is a set of sixteen statements written in a similar format"  
  > -- `research__steering_evaluation_aware_language_models_to_act_l_3180f0ad` (2025-10-23; middle author) 
  > "We think the transcript analysis provides a strong counterargument to this concern, and we are also able to increase the type hint rate by steering in the evaluation direction. Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors"  
  > -- `research__steering_evaluation_aware_language_models_to_act_l_3180f0ad` (2025-10-23; middle author)
